story.title: In 1962, Laughter Shut Down 14 Schools
story.topic: The 1962 Tanganyika laughter epidemic: Kashasha mission girls' boarding school near Bukoba; 95 of 159 pupils; school closed 18 March 1962; spread to Nshamba and other villages; 14 schools closed, about 1,000 people; leading explanation mass psychogenic illness
story.angle: An epidemic whose only symptom was laughter, and it wasn't funny: the cure (sending everyone home) spread it, and there was never a joke
story.centralQuestion: What makes a thousand people laugh without a joke?
story.takeaway: Stress can spread through a community like a disease, even as laughter
story.tone: paradox hook, brisk middle, eerie ending
story.sensitivity: Real distress of real schoolgirls in 1962 Tanganyika: shown with dignity, laughing WITH tears and frightened eyes, never as comedy; no caricature; the cause is framed as the leading explanation, not as a put-down

publishing.description:
On 30 January 1962, at a mission girls' boarding school in Kashasha, near Bukoba on Lake Victoria in newly independent Tanganyika (now Tanzania), three students started laughing and couldn't stop. Within weeks 95 of the school's 159 pupils had attacks: laughing mixed with crying, restlessness and fainting, lasting hours and coming back. Teachers were not affected.

On 18 March the school was closed and the girls were sent home. It spread with them: to Nshamba, where 217 people had attacks, and to other villages and schools. In all, 14 schools were shut and about 1,000 people were affected over roughly a year and a half.

Doctors tested for poison and infection and found neither. The leading explanation is mass psychogenic illness: real physical symptoms, spread socially, triggered by stress. Tanganyika had won independence on 9 December 1961, and pupils lived under strict discipline and heavy expectations. No joke was ever recorded. This is the leading theory, not a settled fact, and some historians question how the case was framed at the time.

Sources:
- A. M. Rankin & P. J. Philip, "An epidemic of laughing in the Bukoba district of Tanganyika", Central African Journal of Medicine, May 1963 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/13973013)
- C. F. Hempelmann, "The laughter of the 1962 Tanganyika 'laughter epidemic'", Humor 20(1), 2007
- Robert Provine, Laughter: A Scientific Investigation; interviewed by Lawrence Weschler (https://lawrenceweschler.substack.com/p/august-3-2023-issue-48)
- Wikipedia, Tanganyika laughter epidemic (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_laughter_epidemic)
- Clio's Current (https://clioscurrent.com/blog/2015/7/29/tanganyikalaughingepidemic)
- Scibabe (https://scibabe.com/daily-mos-the-tanganyika-laughing-epidemic/)
- Owaahh (https://owaahh.com/the-tanganyika-laughing-epidemic-of-1962)
- Now I Know (https://nowiknow.com/tanganyikas-laughing-epidemic/)

publishing.pinnedComment: Poison or the mind? Doctors ruled out poison and infection, and the leading explanation is mass psychogenic illness from stress after independence. Others think something physical was missed, or that the "hysteria" label says more about 1960s medicine than about the girls. Which side are you on? 👇
